title: Cyrus the LORD's shepherd and anointed (Isa 44:24–45:13)
speaker: The LORD (through the prophet)
description: The LORD names Cyrus "my shepherd", who will fulfil his purpose, say of Jerusalem "She will be built" and of the Temple "Your foundation will be laid" (44:28); calls him "his anointed", whose right hand he has held, to subdue nations and open doors and gates (45:1–3), for Israel's sake though Cyrus has not known him (45:4–5); he will build the LORD's city and free the exiles, not for price or reward (45:13).
in_text_interpretation: The text names Cyrus explicitly (44:28; 45:1) and states the purposes: Jerusalem rebuilt, the Temple founded, exiles freed. It does not name Babylon in these verses (cf. 47:1; 48:14).

interpretations.label: Predictive prophecy of Isaiah of Jerusalem, fulfilled by Cyrus (539–538)
proponents: Josephus (Ant. 11.1.1–2: Cyrus read his name in Isaiah, "one hundred and forty years before the temple was demolished")
D. Guzik (more than 200 years before Cyrus's birth; citing Poole and Motyer)
interpretations.summary: Textual reasoning: the book is headed as Isaiah's (1:1), and the passage presents the naming of Cyrus as proof that the LORD foretells (44:24–26). Fulfilment: Cyrus took Babylon (539) and in his first year authorised the return and the Temple (Ezra 1; 2 Chr 36:22–23). Guzik: the name is woven into the poem and cannot be a later insertion; Motyer: no basis to limit prediction. Josephus says Cyrus himself was moved by reading it. Objection: critical scholarship dates the passage to Cyrus's own career (below). Note: the Whiston text of Josephus gives 140 years before the destruction; Guzik (via Bultema) reports 220.

interpretations.label: An exilic prophet announcing Cyrus's imminent conquest (c. 546–539), fulfilled shortly after
proponents: J. Skinner (1898), summarising S. R. Driver
J. C. Döderlein (1775), with Ibn Ezra as a guarded forerunner (per Skinner)
interpretations.summary: Textual reasoning: Cyrus is addressed as an already famous conqueror whose victories have shaken the world (41:2–3, 25) while Babylon's capture is still future (45:2–3; 48:14), so chs. 40–48 date between 550 and 539, almost certainly after the fall of Sardis (546); 46:1 may allude to Nabonidus's moving of the gods in 539 (Sellin, via Skinner). The announced events followed: Babylon fell in 539 and Cyrus's decree allowed the return. Objection: Guzik and Motyer reject the premise that detailed prediction is impossible; Skinner records that the case rests on internal evidence.
